description: The entrance to computing as practiced: software, data, and the web. Networks, security, and infrastructure hang off it in their own clusters.

concepts.title: Computing
concepts.summary: Machines that follow instructions, and the layers people built on top of that one ability: programs, data, networks, and the habits of a world that now runs on them.

concepts.title: Software
concepts.summary: Instructions written so a machine can follow them, layer on layer. Unlike almost anything else people build, it costs nothing to copy and everything to get exactly right.

concepts.title: Programming Languages
concepts.summary: Ways of writing instructions that people can read and machines can run. Each one is a set of choices about what is easy to say and what is easy to get wrong.

concepts.title: Operating Systems
concepts.summary: The program that shares the machine out: memory, processor time, disks, and screens, among everything else that wants them. It's the referee that lets a hundred programs coexist.

concepts.title: APIs
concepts.summary: An agreed way for one program to ask another for something. A good one hides everything messy behind a few clear questions, which is what lets software be built out of parts.

concepts.title: Version Control
concepts.summary: A memory for a project: every change recorded, every earlier state recoverable, and different lines of work able to diverge and merge. Git made it something nearly every developer shares.

concepts.title: Open Source
concepts.summary: Software whose source anyone may read, change, and share. A great deal of the internet runs on code written this way, by people who mostly never met.

concepts.title: Debugging
concepts.summary: Finding out why a program does what it says rather than what was meant. Most of it is careful observation, forming a guess, and testing whether the guess survives.

concepts.title: Data
concepts.summary: Facts written down in a form a machine can store and move. Data isn't knowledge by itself; it's what knowledge is made from once someone decides what it means.

concepts.title: Databases
concepts.summary: Organized memory that many programs can share safely: stored, searched, and updated without losing anything when the power fails or two people write at once.

concepts.title: SQL
concepts.summary: A language for asking a database questions by describing what you want, not how to fetch it. Fifty years old, and still the way most structured data is queried.

concepts.title: Transactions
concepts.summary: A group of changes that either all happen or none do. Moving money between accounts has to work this way, or a failure halfway would make some of it vanish.

concepts.title: Indexes
concepts.summary: A side structure that lets a database find a row without reading the whole table, like the index at the back of a book. It trades extra space and slower writes for much faster lookups.

concepts.title: Caching
concepts.summary: Keep a copy of something expensive close by. Processors, browsers, and servers all do it, betting that what you needed once you'll need again soon, and the hard part is knowing when the copy has gone stale.

concepts.title: JSON
concepts.summary: A plain-text way to write structured data: named fields, lists, numbers, strings. It's easy for people to read and for programs to parse, which is why it became the common language of APIs.

concepts.title: Text Encoding
concepts.summary: Text is stored as numbers, and an encoding is the agreement about which number means which character. Unicode extended that agreement to nearly every writing system, which is why emoji and Arabic can share a file.

concepts.title: Compression
concepts.summary: Shrinking data by removing what's predictable. It works because real information is full of repetition, and it's a direct practical use of entropy: the less surprising the data, the smaller it can get.

concepts.title: The Web
concepts.summary: Pages that link to pages, fetched by a simple request. It's one application that runs on the internet, not the internet itself, and it turned a network for researchers into a public commons.

concepts.title: HTTP
concepts.summary: The conversation the web runs on: a client asks for something by name, a server answers with a status and a body. Deliberately plain, and it carries almost everything you do online.

concepts.title: HTML
concepts.summary: The markup that describes what a page is made of: headings, paragraphs, links, images. It doesn't say how things look, only what they are, and the browser does the rest.

concepts.title: Browsers
concepts.summary: Programs that fetch pages, run their code, and draw the result, while walling each site off from the others. Today's browser is closer to an operating system than a document viewer.

concepts.title: URLs
concepts.summary: A name for anything on the web: which protocol, which machine, which resource. Being able to point at a thing is what let the web link itself together.

concepts.title: WebSockets
concepts.summary: A connection that stays open so a server can push messages to a page the moment something happens, instead of waiting to be asked. Chat apps and live dashboards lean on it.

concepts.title: curl
concepts.summary: A command that talks to a server the way a browser does, but shows you every word. It is the everyday tool for poking at a web service, and a good way to see how names, connections, encryption and requests fit together.
